title: Munition Inventories: An Update Amid Renewed War Risk
text:
Munition Inventories: An Update Amid Renewed War Risk

Photo: U.S. Army photo by Sgt. JaDarius Duncan via DVIDS

Table of Contents
Ballistic Missile DefenseShort-Range Air and Drone DefenseAir-to-AirLong-Range Ground Attack MunitionsShort- and Medium-Range Ground Attack MunitionsBunker BustersAnti-Ship Munitions: Short-, Medium-, and Long-RangeGround MunitionsHow Did We Get Here, and What Comes Next?

Report
by

Mark F. Cancian
and
Chris H. Park

Published November 10, 2026

President Trump has repeatedly threatened renewed conflict with Iran to force a favorable settlement. Iran, in turn, has vowed retaliation. Does the United States have enough munitions to renew the fight? The short answer is yes—against Iran. Against China, there is great concern. Rebuilding inventories will require a multiyear commitment extending beyond the current crisis.Our previous analyses focused on munitions that have been used heavily in the war against Iran and would be important in a war against China. This report updates inventory estimates and situates munitions expended in the Iran war among the full spectrum of U.S. munitions. That broader view shows a more nuanced situation: Some inventories are in good shape, others are not, and a few are critically short.The Department of Defense (DOD) is concerned that every munition used against Iran reduces capability and potentially deterrence against China. This report assesses the warfighting status of these munitions with a war with China as the metric. Munitions of similar characteristics are grouped together. The nine categories, shown in Table 1, cover most conventional U.S. munitions, save for ones where there is no recent unclassified data.

Table 2 shows acquisition status—cost, usage, and recovery time—for munitions with significant usage in the Iran war. Our April and May analyses, “Last Rounds?” and “Rebuilding U.S. Missile Inventory,” detail the calculation and methodology.

Remote Visualization

Four observations stand out from the estimates:Adequacy for Iran: In the 39-day campaign until the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories. Sufficient numbers remain for a renewed conflict with Iran, as administration officials have said.Long Recovery Time: Most munitions take 2–4 years after Congress appropriates the funds to be delivered. Although production rates are increasing, demand exceeds supply—from both the United States and allies—so timelines have lengthened. The problem is not money, assuming Congress continues its support, but time.High Cost: Highly capable munitions are expensive and have been the primary driver of war costs. U.S. forces reached a “point of munitions transition” by the fifth day of Operation Epic Fury, at which point far cheaper short-range munitions—of equivalent precision and explosive mass as exquisite long-range ones—were used in the strike campaign.Variability in Use: Ship-based missile interceptors were used less than ground-based ones likely because destroyers have been stationed outside the Persian Gulf. In-theater surface ship missile inventories are also constrained because missiles can only be reloaded in a port with specialized facilities. The sections below detail the nine categories of munitions. For seven munitions heavily used in the Iran war, two charts are provided to show:inventory status (1) before Operation Epic Fury and (2) today after wartime expenditures and new deliveries from previous budgets, (3) deliveries expected in the current fiscal year, and (4) funding requested for missiles in the FY 2027 budget; andrecovery timeline, with (1) blue bars showing the cumulative additions to U.S. inventory each quarter based on current DOD projections and (2) a dark green line showing the maximum potential inventory growth, assuming industry achieves capacity goal targets set in the framework agreements and then produces at that level. Ballistic Missile DefenseMissile defense interceptors are in critical short supply, with the prewar inventory already considered inadequate for war against China. U.S. forces operate three principal missile defense programs, as the analysis below details. There are no substitutes for these as there are with other munition categories. Only highly specialized munitions can intercept theater ballistic missiles that reach a velocity of 5,000+ mph in their terminal phase. Aircraft and cruise missiles fly at about 800 mph and drones at 150–250 mph.PatriotAn estimated two-thirds of prewar Patriot interceptor inventory have been expended against Iranian ballistic missiles in the past nine months. Few, if any, were used by U.S. forces against one-way attack drones. Transfers to Ukraine have also diminished the U.S. inventory.

Remote Visualization

Lockheed Martin has announced an annual production goal of 2,000—up from around 600 today—under a January 2026 framework agreement with the Trump administration and has since received a contract from the DOD to build production capacity.There will be a lot of competition for newly produced interceptors. In addition to the United States, 18 other countries operate the Patriot. Even before the war, an estimated 1,600 interceptors were in the allied backlog. U.S. coalition partners, who also heavily used Patriot missiles in the Iran war, have bought more. In October, the Trump administration also approved a sale of 500 interceptors to Ukraine, which reportedly has fully run out of its Patriot stock.

Remote Visualization

THAADAround half of the prewar Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) inventory is estimated to have been used in the Iran war. Eight THAAD batteries are operational, with at least two deployed outside the continental United States before the war, in Guam and South Korea. Several batteries have been sent to the Middle East for Operation Epic Fury. The interceptor complements Patriot by intercepting threats at a higher altitude and over a wider area.

Remote Visualization

To address the high THAAD expenditures in the Middle East, the DOD resequenced deliveries of newly produced missiles in 2025 and 2026 to prioritize the U.S. inventory over those of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Under the framework agreement, Lockheed plans to quadruple THAAD interceptor production capacity.

Remote Visualization

Standard MissilesStandard Missiles are a family of surface-to-air missiles launched from vertical launch system cells on destroyers and cruisers. Use of both missiles has been relatively limited, partly because ships have been stationed outside the Persian Gulf. Standard Missile 3 (SM-3) can intercept ballistic missiles. The Missile Defense Agency procures two variants of the missile, Block IB and IIA, with the latter having greater range (2,500 km vs. 700 km), speed (4.5 km/s vs. 3.0 km/s), and cost ($30 million vs. $16 million). Shore-based versions, called “Aegis Ashore,” exist but are not in theater. Standard Missile 6 (SM-6) was designed as a replacement for the Standard Missile 2 for fleet air defense. It has some anti–ballistic missile capabilities against short- and medium-range ballistic missiles.

Remote Visualization

Remote Visualization

The Trump administration’s framework agreement covers both the SM-3 and SM-6, with RTX seeking to increase SM-3 IIA production “2 to 4 times” and grow SM-6 production to 500 per year. Despite relatively low use in the Iran war thus far, inventory recovery will take time due to small orders in recent years.

Remote Visualization

Remote Visualization

Short-Range Air and Drone DefenseFor countering drones and cruise missiles, the U.S. military has developed several low-cost interceptors. Because these have a relatively short range, many systems are needed to cover all forces and bases in a theater.Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS): A helicopter-launched Hydra 70 rocket with a laser seeker.Roadrunner and Coyote: Low-cost interceptor drones that destroy oncoming drones by crashing into them.Merops: A Ukraine-tested interceptor drone, sent to the Gulf in large numbers.Counter Rocket, Artillery, and Mortar System: A radar-controlled rapid-fire gun for close-in protection, based on the Navy’s Phalanx system.Stinger: A short-range infrared-guided missile. Few are available because many were sent to Ukraine, and the production line just restarted after pausing for many years. Several other systems are in development, often coming from nontraditional suppliers with expertise in technology, mass production, and low-cost manufacturing.Air-to-AirA large inventory of air-to-air missiles remains in U.S. inventory. These missiles are launched from U.S. fighters and have a primary mission to intercept adversary aircraft.AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM), $1 million per unit: A radar-guided missile with a range over 20 miles. A longer-range ground-launched version—developed jointly with Norway—is called the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System. It has been extensively supplied to Ukraine, but U.S. fielding has been limited, with the Army opting instead for the Indirect Fire Protection Capability.AIM-9X Sidewinder, $0.4 million per unit: A heat-seeking missile with a shorter range than AMRAAM. It has been repeatedly upgraded since the 1950s, with the current variant, AIM-9X Block II, being procured since FY 2011.

Remote Visualization

In the Iran war, U.S. and coalition forces have used both air-launched missiles against drones. The great cost imbalance—Shahed drones are estimated to cost $0.02–0.05 million each—makes this impractical as a long-term option. These missiles would be used extensively in a war with China against Chinese aircraft and drones. Long-Range Ground Attack MunitionsThese munitions allow firing platforms to launch from outside an adversary’s strongest air defenses. They were heavily used in the early stages of Operation Epic Fury.TomahawkU.S. destroyers and submarines are estimated to have fired around a third of the prewar Tomahawk inventory so far in the Iran war. Tomahawks are fired from sea at ground targets at a range of around 1,000 miles. Ground-launched versions exist but are not in theater.

Remote Visualization

RTX plans to increase annual Tomahawk production to 1,000, with a contract with the DOD signed in August to accelerate deliveries. Inventory recovery, however, will take time due to small orders in the past—on average, 86 missiles per year in the past 10 fiscal years.

Remote Visualization

JASSMU.S. bombers and fighters launched Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSMs), stealthy, air-launched missiles with a 1,000-pound payload. Around a third of the prewar inventory was expended. The missile has been iteratively upgraded over nearly three decades. The baseline JASSM has a range of 200+ miles, the Extended Range variant (JASSM-ER) has a 500-plus-mile range, and the Extreme Range variant (JASSM-XR) is speculated to have a range of around 1,000 miles.

Remote Visualization

U.S. forces began the campaign in Iran with a large JASSM inventory, and sizable procurement in previous years will rapidly restock the diminished inventory.

Remote Visualization

PrSMOperation Epic Fury was the first combat use of the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), a ground-launched missile used by field artillery systems such as the Multiple Launch Rocket System and the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System. It has a longer range than its predecessor, the Army Tactical Missile System (over 300 miles vs. 180 miles).

Remote Visualization

The prewar inventory for PrSM was low, as procurement began in FY 2023 and first delivery was in early 2026. Large orders from the Army in the queue—964 missiles between FY 2024 and 2026—will quickly replenish stocks and increase inventories greatly.

Remote Visualization

Short- and Medium-Range Ground Attack MunitionsThe United States has large numbers of munitions with the same explosive yield and accuracy as the long-range systems described above but with ranges under 300 miles. Thus, even if long-range ground attack munitions run low, the United States could continue the fight. Air superiority is required to use them extensively, however, as the shorter ranges put launch platforms in danger. These munitions include:Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM), $66,000 per unit plus the cost of the bomb: A guidance kit that gives “dumb” bombs the ability to hit targets precisely. The kit is field-installed on 500-, 1,000-, and 2,000-lb general-purpose bombs. Inventories ran low during the counter-ISIS campaign, which prompted a bump in procurement beginning in FY 2016. It is by far the most used ground attack munition.Joint Air-to-Ground Missile (JAGM), $249,000 per unit: Replacement of the Hellfire for attack helicopters and Reaper-like drones and replaces Maverick for fixed-wing aircraft.Small Diameter Bomb (SDB) I and II, $67,000 and $265,000, respectively, per unit: air-launched, precision-guided glide bombs. SDB II allows attacks on moving targets. The shorter range makes these munitions much less expensive. To illustrate the cost/range trade-off, a JASSM and a BLU-110 bomb fitted with a JDAM guidance kit both accurately deliver 1,000-pound payloads. The JDAM has a maximum range of 15 miles and costs about $100,000, while the JASSM has a range of 600 miles and costs $2.4 million.

Remote Visualization

General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, stated that U.S. forces had reached a “point of munitions transition” to attack Iran “from standoff…to stand-in” by the fifth day of the campaign. By that, Caine meant that early strikes used long-range and expensive munitions to stay outside Iranian air defenses until these defenses were reduced to an acceptable level. Strikes then transitioned to lower-cost munitions. By day 14, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared that less than 1 percent of munitions fired by U.S. forces were long-range. Figure 17 illustrates the change in the munition mix over time.

Remote Visualization

A renewed air campaign would likely follow this pattern. The United States would need to reestablish air superiority because Iran has had time to rebuild its air defenses. The transition to less expensive munitions might occur more quickly. A rebuilt Iranian air defense would be weaker than at the war’s beginning, and U.S. forces have periodically attacked these sites as Iran rebuilt. A faster transition would reduce the use of scarce, high-end munitions.Although this transition is achievable against regional adversaries such as Iran, it may not be achievable against a great power like China. Extensive air defenses of the People’s Liberation Army would take much longer to reduce and might have enough continuing capability to prevent short-range munitions from being used widely. Bunker BustersBunker busters are munitions designed to strike what DOD calls hard and deeply buried targets. A previous analysis discussed these munitions in depth and how they moved from a niche capability into the mainstream as adversaries have learned to tunnel and harden facilities to mitigate the effects of precision strike. Conventional U.S. bunker buster munitions available today come in five general kinds: 500 lb, 2,000 lb, 5,000 lb, very large, and standoff. Most of these are air-dropped bombs (bomb live units, or BLUs) that can be fitted with laser or GPS guidance kits to be configured as guided bomb units (GBUs).

Remote Visualization

The 2,000-lb varieties are plentiful, but the larger bombs have a more limited inventory. The DOD is working to replenish munitions used in Operation Midnight Hammer. All these munitions will face greater demand as the number of hard and deeply buried targets expands. The president reportedly is considering using the “Mother of All Bombs” (MOAB) against Pickaxe Mountain, though the munition may not be able to fully damage the nuclear program facility buried deep inside the mountain. Anti-Ship Munitions: Short-, Medium-, and Long-RangeThese munitions played little role in the Iran war because the Iranian navy was quickly and easily destroyed.

Remote Visualization

These munitions would play a major role in a conflict against China because of its large and highly capable navy. In CSIS wargames, U.S. players typically send bombers based outside China’s missile range to fire long-range anti-ship missiles—long-range platforms firing long-range missiles to stay outside China’s defensive zone. In the early phases of such a conflict, in particular, China’s defenses make close approach suicidal. Ground MunitionsThe Biden administration transferred large quantities of artillery shells, rockets, and anti-tank missiles from U.S. inventory to Ukraine, eventually capping transfers to maintain the minimums needed for U.S. war plans. Inventories have been rebuilding as most transfers ended when the second Trump administration came into office, though newly produced weapons under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List continue to flow to Ukraine. The Iran war has not used any of these munitions because there has so far been no ground combat. This category of munitions would probably not be used extensively in a U.S.-China conflict.The Javelin anti-tank missile illustrates the current situation of this munitions category: Large inventory existed before the Ukraine war, but many (about 40 percent for Javelin) were transferred to Ukraine. Inventories are rebuilding now, with large procurements that began in the Biden administration and continue in the Trump administration.

Remote Visualization

How Did We Get Here, and What Comes Next?Despite criticisms to the contrary, the munitions industrial base was not neglected, nor were previous administrations blind to future needs. The munitions situation today is the result of conscious and rational decisions in national security strategy and acquisition policy. A previous analysis laid out the reasons for low inventories:The post–Cold War strategy required fewer munitions. Instead of an extended global war, the United States planned for short, regional conflicts.The industrial base was designed for efficient peacetime production, not surge. Wars were assumed to be short, and surge capability was regarded as wasteful.Munitions competed poorly in the Pentagon’s budget process. The military services preferred to buy platforms like tanks, aircraft, or ships that were visible and thus could have a more direct deterrent effect on adversaries.The war against Iran and other recent operations have used some munitions extensively. Note, however, that usage is not necessarily bad; munitions exist to be used.Transfers to Ukraine were the major reason for depletion of ground munitions. However, of the 102 line items transferred, only Patriot has been used extensively in the Iran war. Although the current munitions shortage arose from rational choices in the past, a changed environment requires new approaches.Building more started several years ago when the war in Ukraine showed how quickly inventories of weapons, munitions, and supplies would be exhausted in an intense conflict. The Trump administration has accelerated that effort. Production of Patriot missiles is an example. Before the war in Ukraine, production was around 300 per year with half going to the United States and half to allies and partners. Now production is around 600 per year, with a goal of 2,000 per year by 2030.The DOD cannot afford to build adequate inventories by relying solely on highly capable and expensive munitions and thus needs a mix of munitions. Some situations require exquisite capabilities, but many do not. A munitions with a range of capabilities and costs need to be developed and then ushered into production.The nation finally needs to make a long-term commitment to building these inventories by funding them in FY 2027 and beyond. Multiyear commitments convince industry to invest its own money. Industry’s nightmare is that the DOD makes deep cuts in munitions procurement when the current crises ease, leaving industry with unused capacity. Although Congress seems unlikely to pass the DOD’s full FY 2027 request of $1.5 trillion, funding for munitions has had strong bipartisan support and could be given priority.This report is made possible by general support to CSIS.
